summary: Defines extensions to WebDAV for accessing, managing, and sharing contact information in vCard format. It gives a standard way for clients to work with address books stored on a server.

eli5.summary: CardDAV lets your phone and computer keep one shared address book on a server, so adding a friend in one place shows up everywhere.

questions: what is the carddav addressbook-query report
subtitle: How address books of vCard contacts are stored, searched and shared on a WebDAV server.

tldr.problem: Email, calendar and messaging clients all need remote access to contact data, and the older protocols for that (LDAP, IMSP, ACAP, SyncML) each had their own costs for design, testing and deployment.
tldr.mechanism: CardDAV models an address book as a WebDAV collection holding one vCard per resource, adds two search reports (query and multiget), and builds on WebDAV access control and HTTP entity tags for sharing and safe updates.
tldr.outcome: It gives clients a standard way to read, search, write and share address books over HTTP with TLS. RFC 6764 later updated this document.

today: RFC 6352 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6764. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Address Books Use WebDAV
sections.content:
RFC 6352 defines CardDAV, a set of extensions to WebDAV for accessing, managing and sharing contact information in the vCard format. Before it, remote contact access used protocols such as LDAP, the Internet Message Support Protocol (IMSP) and the Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP), with SyncML used for synchronization.

The RFC lists what WebDAV brings: several address books in a hierarchy, access control per address book and per entry, server-side searching so a client need not download a whole address book for a quick address expansion, internationalization through XML, vCard as a well-defined schema, and an HTTP stack that even limited mobile clients already have.

The one key disadvantage it names is the lack of change notification. The RFC notes that many alternative protocols lack it too, and that a push-notification extension could easily be developed.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a brand new way to talk to a server, CardDAV reuses the web's existing file-sharing rules. That makes it cheaper to build and easier for small devices to use.

sections.title: What a CardDAV Server Must Support
sections.content:
To advertise CardDAV support, a server MUST support vCard v3 as the media type for address objects, WebDAV Class 3, and WebDAV ACL (RFC 3744). It must also support secure transport using TLS, entity tags with the extra rules in section 6.3.2.3, and all the address book reports in section 8, and it must advertise those reports in the DAV:supported-report-set property.

A server SHOULD additionally support vCard v4 (RFC 6350), the extended MKCOL method (RFC 5689) and the DAV:current-user-principal-URL property (RFC 5397).

A server announces support by including addressbook in the DAV response header of an OPTIONS request on any resource that supports address book properties, reports or methods.
sections.eli5: Before a server can say it speaks CardDAV, it has to pass a checklist: it must handle contact cards, keep conversations private with TLS, and know how to search.

sections.title: Address Books and Address Objects
sections.content:
A CardDAV address book is a WebDAV collection with a defined structure. Each direct child is an address object resource, and each of those and each collection can be locked and can carry its own properties. The server is the canonical location for address data, and clients may store data offline and synchronize later, so entity tags and locking help detect changes.

Each address object resource MUST contain a single vCard component only, and its UID property MUST be unique within the address book collection. An address book collection reports both DAV:collection and CARDDAV:addressbook in its DAV:resourcetype. It may contain only address object resources and ordinary collections, and address book collections cannot be nested at any depth.

Servers can support more than one media type, for example vCard 3.0 and 4.0, and advertise them in CARDDAV:supported-address-data. Without that property a server accepts only text/vcard version 3.0. Clients can use the HTTP Accept header to ask for a particular format, and if the server cannot convert it returns the CARDDAV:supported-address-data-conversion precondition.
sections.eli5: An address book is like a folder, and every contact is one card inside it. Each card needs its own unique ID, and you cannot put a folder-of-address-books inside another address book.

sections.title: Creating and Updating Contacts
sections.content:
A new address book is created with the extended MKCOL method, setting DAV:resourcetype and optionally DAV:displayname and CARDDAV:addressbook-description. Support is only RECOMMENDED because some stores offer one pre-created address book per user.

New contacts are created with PUT to an unused URL. Clients SHOULD send If-None-Match: * so they cannot overwrite an existing resource by accident. Updates use If-Match with the stored entity tag. The URL is arbitrary, though file names are commonly suffixed .vcf.

The RFC adds preconditions for PUT, COPY and MOVE: a supported media type, valid vCard data, no UID conflict, a valid copy or move destination and a size within CARDDAV:max-resource-size. Servers MUST accept non-standard X- properties and parameters, and DAV:getetag MUST be a strong entity tag on every address object resource.
sections.eli5: To add a contact you put a new card in the folder, and you say 'only if there is no card with this name yet'. To change a card you say 'only if it is still the version I saw', so you never erase a friend's edit.

sections.title: Searching with Reports
sections.content:
Servers MUST support two REPORT methods on address books. Both return a DAV:multistatus body, and both let the client name the WebDAV properties and the vCard properties it wants back, so large items such as an inline PHOTO can be skipped.

CARDDAV:addressbook-query searches for address objects matching a CARDDAV:filter. The filter contains prop-filter elements (and optionally param-filter), with text-match using equals, contains, starts-with or ends-with. The request MUST include a Depth header. A client can cap results with CARDDAV:limit; when a result set is truncated the server uses status 207 and reports 507 (Insufficient Storage) for the Request-URI.

CARDDAV:addressbook-multiget fetches specific resources by a list of DAV:href elements and uses Depth: 0. A missing resource gets an error status in its own response element, such as 404.

Text matching uses collations from the IANA registry. Servers are required to support i;ascii-casemap and i;unicode-casemap, and i;unicode-casemap is the default.
sections.eli5: A report is like asking the librarian a question: 'bring me every card where the nickname is me', or 'bring me exactly these three cards'. The server does the searching so your phone does not have to carry the whole book.

sections.title: Client Guidelines and Discovery
sections.content:
Clients are advised to request only the properties they need, but to change a vCard they must PUT the whole thing, since there is no incremental edit. They SHOULD use If-Match to avoid lost updates, and on a precondition failure they reload and merge before writing again.

For setup, the key piece of information is the user's principal URL. With SRV records and DAV:current-user-principal-URL, a user only needs to enter a user identifier, host name and password. The client looks up the server with SRV, then sends an authenticated PROPFIND to find the principal URL, and from there the CARDDAV:addressbook-home-set property leads to the address books.

Section 11 adds two SRV service types: carddav for HTTP without TLS and carddavs for HTTP with TLS. To find another user's address book, the RFC suggests the DAV:principal-property-search report from RFC 3744.
sections.eli5: To set up your phone you only type your name, the server's name and your password. The phone then follows a trail of clues on the server until it finds your address books.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HTTP traffic is sent in the clear unless TLS is used. If HTTP Basic authentication is available, the server MUST allow TLS at the same time and SHOULD prevent Basic authentication when TLS is not in use. Clients SHOULD use TLS whenever possible.

Address books can be private, shared or public through WebDAV ACL. Servers MUST apply the correct privileges when provisioning each kind, and private and shared address books MUST NOT be accessible to unauthenticated users, to keep web crawlers from indexing them. Clients SHOULD warn users when they copy or move data from a private address book to a shared or public one, and when changes would open a private or shared address book to unauthenticated users.

The specification relies on standard HTTP authentication: Basic, Digest, and TLS with client certificates.
sections.eli5: Your contacts are private, so the conversation should be locked with TLS and private books must stay closed to strangers. Apps should also warn you before you move a card into a book other people can see.
